Comments to the Authors:

We are sorry to say that, after consultation with the reviewers, we have decided that this work will not be considered further for publication by eLife.

Overall, the reviewers thought the study was of interest and had the potential to provide novel insights into how cell-matrix and cell-cell interactions contribute to the development and function of pancreatic islets. However, there were several issues raised about experimental numbers, statistical analysis, and image quality. Additional experiments would also be needed to support the conclusions related to the role of hypoxia and cell-ECM interactions. There is also a need for a more extensive analysis of the RNA-Seq data and rationale for following up on CTNNA1. More extensive analysis is especially important given some of the discrepancies of this study's findings/interpretations with past studies in the literature.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors of this manuscript conducted a series of sophisticated gene deletion experiments that aimed to understand the relative contribution of cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions in the development and function of pancreatic islets. Despite the importance of the questions being asked in their study, the data are over-interpreted, and some conclusions are not supported by the data presented or by the current literature on the subject. Specific examples include the misinterpretation of basic mechanisms of cell interactions such as the model of differential adhesion suggesting that Ctnna1-null β-cells merge into the core of islet clusters due to weaker adhesion. The model proposed by Foty and Steinberg (validated in numerous developing epithelia) predicts the opposite, i.e. cells with weaker adhesion are pushed outward by cells with stronger adhesion.

In experiments reporting on the phenotype of double KO animals in which both α-catenin and beta1 integrin were simultaneously deleted, the interpretation of the results is clearly affected by the profound alterations of cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions, making it difficult to draw conclusions about normal pancreas development.

Strengths include the sophisticated animal models permitting cell lineage tracing experiments for live imaging, and state-of-the-art techniques used for the analysis of the pancreatic phenotype. However, the manuscript presents data that are either incompletely analyzed or insufficient to support the authors' claims. As a result, it is unlikely that this study, in its current presentation, will significantly advance our knowledge of the function of these two distinct mechanisms of cell interactions in pancreas development.

The authors of this manuscript conducted a series of sophisticated gene deletion experiments that aimed to understand the relative contribution of cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions in the development and function of pancreatic islets.

Despite the importance of the questions being asked in their study, as presented, the manuscript presents several weaknesses.

Specific examples are listed below:

The cell lineage tracing experiments with the mT/mG reporter are superficially described, and the data presented are not vetted by solid statistical analysis.

The authors do not provide any information about the number of mice studied for each animal model, the number of tissue sections stained and analyzed, number of experiments performed. This is critical information that should be provided both in the methods and in the legend of the figures.

Most immunofluorescence images provided in the figures are oversaturated, making it difficult to discriminate, at least qualitatively, levels of expression of the different markers.

In Figure 2, data shown in panel N are difficult to interpret given the large scale on the Y axis, for the relatively low counts reported in the plot. Is it really possible to have a *** statistical significance between control cells and integrin beta1 KO when the values are almost identical? What type of statistical method was used? It is also unclear how many of such experiments were performed (n=?).

In the manuscript, (lines 433-435), the authors state: "… ECM-Integrin signaling is critical for endocrine cell migration, and that the time window for endocrine cell initiation is small." According to the data presented, and some of the literature cited, it is the "endocrine progenitors" and not the "endocrine cells" that rely on the ECM-Integrin signaling for cell migration. It is also inaccurate to state that ECM-Integrin signaling does not occur in endocrine cells once they have differentiated. Thus, while the function of this interaction may or may not translate into cell migration, integrin signaling continues to play important roles in differentiated cells in multiple tissues.

Experiments conducted with the Ucn3-Cre;Itgb1f/f mice are superficially described. A more detailed presentation and discussion of the phenotype of these mice is necessary to draw conclusions about the role of Itgb1 in β cells after they have differentiated. This is especially important for comparison with other studies if one considers that could reveal important information compared to previous studies that used the insulin promoter as a driver of Cre. This is important since the Ucn3 and Insulin genes are expressed at different times and at different levels during β cell development.

The RNA-seq data, although interesting, are only superficially analyzed, nor validated. Experiments of immunofluorescence do not really validate the most interesting alterations of genes found affected by the gene deletions, since it is not very quantitative. It would have been helpful to confirm at the protein level by Western blotting the expression of some of the most interesting genes, or at least by qPCR. The authors would be surprised to discover that RNA-seq does not necessarily translate into the same order of magnitude of mRNA levels when testing the same samples by qPCR.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

The goal of this study was to uncover mechanisms that govern the aggregation and "self-assembly" of islets during embryonic development and postnatally, a process that is not well understood. The authors focused on the role of integrin-β 1 (Itgb1), a key mediator of cell-extracellular matrix (ECM) interactions, and on α-catenin (Ctnna1), a hub protein that links cell adhesion molecules with the cytoskeleton. They used conditional knockout models (Ngn3-Cre and Ucn3-Cre), microscopy and morphometric image analysis, and transcriptomic, and functional measures of glucose metabolism. They found that loss of Itgb1 from endocrine precursor cells resulted in premature aggregation of islets and impaired migration of islets from pancreatic ducts resulting in disturbed islet morphology. Additionally, they observed loss of islet vascularization and decreased expression of markers of endocrine cell identity, which together resulted in glucose intolerance. On the other hand, loss of Ctnna1 resulted in smaller, hypervascularized islets which also expressed fewer markers of differentiated endocrine cell identity resulting in an age-dependent loss of glucose tolerance. Ctnna1 mice also exhibited loss of glucagon and somatostatin-positive islets cells, with loss of glucagon+ cells occurring postnatally. The authors concluded from these studies that a balance exists between cell-ECM and cell-cell interactions, and that loss of one of these interactions (as occurs in Itgb1 and Ctnna1 deficient mice, respectively) may result in an increase in the other. However, the loss of both Itgb1 and Ctnna1 from endocrine precursor cells resulted in an almost complete loss of islet aggregation and severe glucose intolerance.

The conclusions of this paper are mostly supported by the data. Strengths include the thorough characterization of mice, especially the Itgb1 mice with the Ngn3-Cre driver. The work shows a clear effect of both Itgb1 and Ctnna1 to modulate islet aggregation/morphology without affecting cell specification or overall abundance (during development). The study provides compelling evidence for the role of these cell adhesion molecules in governing islet aggregation, morphology, identity, and function and is impactful for the field.

The weaknesses are generally minor, with support for some statements being made using a small amount of data (single images in some cases); although most of these do not detract from the main message of the work. For the in vitro aggregation study in the Itgb1 deficient cells, while true that these cells seem to be able to form small aggregates after short-term plating on ECM, further aggregation was inhibited. This illustrates that other mediators of cell-ECM interactions may also be important, a point that was not fully acknowledged in this study. The work on cell shape and cell-cell adhesion in the Itgb1 mice is not as strongly supported by data as the other components of that work. For the Ctnna1 work, the details regarding F-actin localization are hard to appreciate from the images provided. The concept that glucagon+ cells may undergo cell death due to detachment from surrounding cells is exciting, but it is not clear whether the current data fully support that hypothesis.

Together, these data show that both cell-ECM and cell-cell interactions are critical for normal aggregation, morphology, and vascularization of islets and that disturbances in either, or both, have substantial effects on cell identity and function. This work will be impactful for the islet biology field.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

Pancreatic islet morphogenesis is a complex interplay between endocrine cell-intrinsic signaling coupled with external cues from ECM and neighboring cells. Defining the specific pathways and the developmental window when they are critical to the eventual islet architecture and function still remains unclear. This study adds to the body of evidence that the ECM-Integrin signaling and cell-cell adhesion signaling mediated via α-catenin has a critical combinatorial role in determining the islet cell aggregation, vascularization, and eventual function.

Strengths:

The reciprocal regulation of the ECM-integrin pathway and cell-cell adhesion via the α-catenin pathway identified in this study provides insight into how the external cues for developing endocrine cells are processed and integrated to eventually allow mouse islets to develop a core of β-cells and the mantle comprising of other endocrine cells. The detailed dissection to identify the developmental window using in vivo studies complemented with explant studies with lineage tracing is compelling strength of this study.

The predicted changes in mouse islet (mantle-core) architecture due to changes in cell-cell adhesion strength as validated by the combination of the models that the authors use in this study provides a better understanding of the dynamics of islet morphogenesis.

Weakness:

The authors suggest that hypoxia resulting from changes in the vasculature is a potential cause of functional immaturity stemming from the expression of disallowed genes and enrichment of genes in RNA-seq involved in Hypoxic responses. Experimental demonstration of hypoxia and its causative role in these models is however lacking to substantiate this explanation.

Many other groups have previously demonstrated the importance of α-catenin and β-integrin 1 in islet morphogenesis and function, using earlier (Pdx1 promoter-driven Cre) and later (various insulin promoter-driven Cre) developmental windows. Though this study narrows down the window to when the endocrine lineage is determined by Ngn3 and suggests that the altered cell adhesion leads to changes in function and aggregation, intracellular signaling pathways suggested by other studies, such as the sonic hedgehog pathway, PARP, and others remain unexplored in the current context to provide more mechanistic insight.

While the regulation of the vascularization of the islets in both these mutant models (Itfb1 and Ctnna1) individually and in combination is very convincing, the authors note that this was with no change in angiogenic factor expression. While their explanation invoking the alterations of cortical tension by changes in actin cytoskeleton is certainly plausible and intriguing, it is not demonstrated experimentally and remains to be established in future work.

1. Concurrent measurement of insulin and glucose during the GTT provides compelling evidence of a β-cell defect. Adding this with the GTT data in Figures 1, 4, and S6 would add to the strength of the study.

2. The glucose and functional phenotype of the Ucn-Cre mediated Itgb1ΔMatureβ/ΔMatureβ has not been described. Since this is a new model generated by the authors, it is important to describe the phenotype and also compare and contrast it to the other previously described mature β-cell ITGB knockouts that the authors allude to in their discussion.

results.result: Islet endocrine cell-specific inactivation of integrin β1 (Itgb1ΔEndo/ΔEndo) disrupts blood vessel interactions, promotes cell-cell adhesion, and results in larger islets with aberrant distribution of α- and δ-cells, profoundly impacting islet morphogenesis without affecting endocrine cell fate choice.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C43-C45, C48-C50 collectively demonstrate that Itgb1 deletion disrupts vascular attachment (electron microscopy, C44-C45), increases islet size (morphometric analysis, C48), and alters cell distribution (C49) while maintaining normal endocrine cell proportions (C46-C47). The conclusion that Itgb1 affects morphogenesis but not fate choice (C50) is well-supported by converging evidence from multiple imaging modalities and quantification.

results.result: Loss of Itgb1 in endocrine cells leads to reduced vascularization, hypoxia responses, down-regulation of β-cell maturation genes, up-regulation of disallowed genes, and functional impairment including glucose intolerance and reduced insulin secretion that worsens with age.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C63 provide comprehensive evidence from RNA-seq (417 DEGs, C51-C52), pathway analysis (hypoxia, C53-C54), immunofluorescence validation (C55, C58), and functional assays (glucose tolerance tests, insulin secretion, C61-C62). The inference that reduced vascularization causes hypoxia (C56) is reasonable given the correlation, though causality is not directly tested. The conclusion about ECM-integrin importance (C63) is well-supported by the totality of evidence.

results.result: Itgb1-deficient endocrine cells show premature aggregation within ductal cords during development, with larger isolated islets but unchanged total islet area, suggesting morphological changes independent of total endocrine cell expansion and deficiencies in migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C71, C73 demonstrate that Itgb1 deletion affects islet size distribution (C64, C66) without changing total islet area (C65, C67), increases ductal cell content in islets (C68-C69), and impairs migration (C70-C71) based on 3D segmentation and live imaging. The timing-dependent effect (C73) is supported by comparison with later-stage deletions (C72). The inference about morphological vs. proliferative changes (C67) is reasonable given the data.

results.result: ECM-Itgb1 signaling negatively regulates islet cell-cell adhesion, as evidenced by increased E-cadherin clusters in Itgb1-deficient islets, enhanced aggregation in vitro even in the presence of ECM, and increased F-actin condensation at cell junctions.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C83 provide converging evidence from super-resolution imaging (increased Ecad+ clusters, C74-C75), in vitro aggregation assays (C77-C80), and F-actin analysis (C82). The conclusion that Itgb1 negatively regulates cell adhesion (C76, C81) is well-supported by multiple independent assays. The inference about actin cytoskeleton alterations (C83) is reasonable given the F-actin data, though the mechanism is not fully elucidated.

results.result: Ablation of α-catenin (Ctnna1ΔEndo/ΔEndo) in endocrine progenitors results in smaller average islet size with unchanged total islet area, reduced E-cadherin expression, decreased F-actin density at cell junctions, and disrupted cell adhesion.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C89 demonstrate that Ctnna1 deletion reduces islet size (C85-C86) without affecting total islet mass (C84, C87), and show reduced Ecad and F-actin (C88) by Airyscan imaging. The inference about disrupted cell adhesion (C89) is well-supported by the molecular data. The conclusion that Ctnna1 is required for aggregation but not total islet mass (C87) is consistent with the quantitative data.

results.result: Inactivation of Ctnna1 in endocrine progenitors leads to up-regulation of ECM signaling and blood vessel interaction genes, increased islet vascularization (observed as early as P14), abnormal F-actin organization, and compromised endocrine cell aggregation, demonstrating that the balance between cell-cell adhesion and blood vessel interaction is crucial for islet development.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C99 provide comprehensive evidence from RNA-seq (319 DEGs with up-regulated ECM/vascular genes, C90-C91), immunofluorescence validation of increased vasculature (C93-C94), and F-actin imaging (C96-C97). The conclusion about the importance of balancing cell-cell adhesion and vascular interaction (C99) is well-supported by the contrasting phenotypes of Itgb1 and Ctnna1 deletions. The temporal data (P14, C94, C97) strengthens the developmental interpretation.

results.result: Ctnna1ΔEndo/ΔEndo mice show down-regulation of genes required for glycemic control and up-regulation of disallowed β-cell genes, mild glucose intolerance at 8 weeks that worsens with age, and a trend toward reduced insulin secretion, indicating that Ctnna1-dependent islet aggregation is crucial for β-cell function and glucose homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C107 demonstrate gene expression changes (C100-C101), glucose intolerance (C103, C106), and trends in insulin secretion (C105) using multiple assays including RNA-seq, qPCR, glucose tolerance tests, and hyperglycemic clamps. The lack of significant insulin secretion defects in conventional assays (C104) but trends in more sensitive clamps (C105) is appropriately noted. The conclusion about Ctnna1's importance for β-cell function (C107) is supported, though the functional defects are relatively mild at 8 weeks.

results.result: Ctnna1ΔEndo/ΔEndo islets show severe reduction of α-cell and δ-cell populations in adulthood despite normal cell numbers at P0 and P7, with α-cell detachment from islet mantles by P7 and three-fold increased apoptosis, demonstrating that Ctnna1 is required for α-cell survival rather than differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C119 provide strong evidence from RNA-seq (down-regulated α- and δ-cell genes, C108), immunofluorescence quantification (severe reduction in adults, C111; normal at P0/P7, C112), electron microscopy (cell detachment, C114-C116), and TUNEL assays (3× increased apoptosis, C117). The temporal analysis (C112-C113) effectively rules out differentiation defects, and the apoptosis data (C117-C118) provides a mechanism. The conclusion (C119) is well-supported by the developmental time course.

results.result: Cell adhesion molecules (E-cadherin, N-cadherin, α-catenin, β-catenin) are expressed at higher levels in β-cells than in α- and δ-cells, with β-cells showing strong F-actin condensed junctions and α-cells displaying loosely bundled F-actin, suggesting differential adhesive properties between endocrine subtypes consistent with the differential adhesion hypothesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C128 combine re-analysis of published gene expression data (C120) with Airyscan imaging of F-actin organization (C124-C125, C127). The inference about differential adhesive properties (C121, C126) is reasonable given the molecular and structural data. The reference to the differential adhesion hypothesis (C122) provides theoretical context. The observation that Ctnna1 deletion reduces F-actin in both cell types (C127-C128) supports the role of α-catenin in adhesion assembly.

results.result: Cell-type-specific deletion of Ctnna1 in β-cells (Ctnna1Δβ/Δβ) or α-cells (Ctnna1Δα/Δα) reveals that differential adhesion between endocrine subtypes contributes to islet architecture, with β-cell-specific deletion causing α-cells to relocate to the core and cluster, while α-cell-specific deletion causes α-cells to scatter as single cells in the core, suggesting more complex regulation than simple differential adhesion.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C135 provide evidence from cell-type-specific deletions with quantification of α-cell localization (C129, C131). The Ctnna1Δβ/Δβ results (C129-C130) are consistent with differential adhesion hypothesis predictions, but the Ctnna1Δα/Δα results (C131-C132) show unexpected scattering rather than clustering. The inference that regulation is more complex than simple DAH (C133) is appropriate given the unexpected findings. The conclusion about differential adhesion contributing to architecture (C134-C135) is supported, though the mechanism is more nuanced than initially hypothesized.

results.result: At P7, double knockout (DKO) of Ctnna1 and Itgb1 completely abrogates endocrine cell aggregation, resulting in scattered single cells with rounded morphology, weak F-actin assemblies, and altered vascular interactions, while endocrine cell subtypes remain present, suggesting that differentiation is independent of aggregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C143 demonstrate the severe phenotype of simultaneous deletion using immunofluorescence (C136-C140) and Airyscan imaging (C141). The observation that cell types are still present (C142) despite complete loss of aggregation supports the inference that differentiation is independent of aggregation (C143). The contrasting phenotypes of single deletions (C136-C138) vs. double deletion (C139-C141) effectively demonstrate the complementary roles of the two adhesion systems.

results.result: Deletion of Ctnna1 or Itgb1 in endocrine progenitors reduces expression of β-cell maturation markers (Ucn3, Glut2) at P7, with DKO showing severe loss of maturation markers and elevated expression of progenitor markers (Sox9, Spp1), suggesting that β-cell maturation is linked to cell adhesion-mediated islet aggregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C147 demonstrate reduced maturation markers in single deletions (C144) and severe loss in DKO (C145) by immunofluorescence, along with inappropriate progenitor marker expression in DKO (C146). The inference that maturation is linked to aggregation (C147) is well-supported by the correlation between aggregation defects and maturation defects across the three genotypes. The P7 timepoint is appropriate for assessing early maturation.

results.result: At 8 weeks, DKO mice show persistent defects in islet aggregation and β-cell maturation, with scattered endocrine cells expressing progenitor markers, complete separation of cells without junction structures, separation from vasculature, low expression of maturation markers, severe glucose intolerance, and very low insulin secretion, demonstrating that islet morphogenesis, vascular interaction, aggregation, and β-cell maturation depend on cell-ECM and cell-cell adhesion during development.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C156 provide comprehensive evidence that DKO defects persist into adulthood using immunofluorescence (C148-C149, C153), super-resolution imaging (C150-C151), and functional assays (C154-C155). The conclusion (C156) integrates findings from all genotypes and timepoints. The persistence of defects from P7 to 8 weeks (C152) demonstrates that these are not developmental delays. The severe functional impairment (C154-C155) validates the biological significance of the morphological defects.

results.result: Background knowledge about pancreatic islet structure, development, and the roles of cell adhesion molecules and ECM-integrin signaling in various tissues, establishing the context for investigating islet aggregation mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C10-C37 represent established knowledge and prior work cited from the literature. These claims provide appropriate context for the study and are supported by citations to relevant research. The claims accurately represent the state of knowledge about islet development, cell adhesion molecules (N-CAM, E-cadherin, α-catenin, β-catenin), and ECM-integrin signaling in various developmental contexts.

results.result: At E15.5, endocrine cells have started aggregating with highly similar vascular and ductal networks, and both Ngn3+ endocrine progenitors and their progeny express Itgb1, with ECM-Itgb1 signaling genes enriched in Ngn3+ cells, suggesting blood vessels could provide instructive cues for islet aggregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C38, C42 are supported by imaging data (whole-mount IF, confocal microscopy). Claim C41 is supported by citation to published single-cell RNA-seq data. The inference that blood vessels could provide instructive cues (C39) is reasonable given the spatial relationship and molecular data, though it remains speculative. Claim C40 is supported by citations. The evidence collectively supports investigating the role of ECM-Itgb1 signaling in islet development.

results.result: All four endocrine cell subtypes (α, β, δ, Ppy) are present at similar proportions in control and Itgb1ΔEndo/ΔEndo islets, and β-cell lineage markers Nkx6.1 and Pdx1 are expressed in Ins+ cells of both genotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 are supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification. This demonstrates that Itgb1 deletion does not affect endocrine cell fate specification or lineage marker expression, which is important for interpreting the morphological and functional defects as being due to aggregation/adhesion rather than differentiation problems.

results.result: Previous studies using Ins-Cre or RIP-Cre to ablate Itgb1 after differentiation into insulin-producing cells did not report aggregation or migration defects, but Ngn3-Cre-mediated deletion occurs earlier in embryonic stages, suggesting Itgb1 regulates migration and aggregation of endocrine progenitors during islet development.
results.evaluation: Claim C72 accurately cites prior work showing no defects with later-stage deletion. The inference (C73) that timing matters is reasonable given the contrasting phenotypes and the known timing of Ngn3-Cre expression (C42). This comparison strengthens the interpretation that Itgb1 functions specifically during the progenitor stage to regulate migration and aggregation.
